title: The New Hampshire Confession (Condensed)
subtitle: The New Hampshire Confession of Faith (1833), faithfully condensed article by article, the confession behind most American Baptist church covenants.
intro:
By the 1830s, Baptists in New England were caught between two fires. On one side stood the older Calvinism of the 1689 tradition, which some found stated too severely. On the other, the Free Will Baptists were growing fast by preaching against it. The Baptist Convention of New Hampshire asked for a statement of faith that ordinary churches could actually use, and the task fell finally to John Newton Brown, who completed the text in 1833. The result is moderate, brief, and deliberately calm. Calvinist in its bones, but stated in language a revival-era congregation could own without a fight.

No confession has shaped more American Baptist churches. Through its inclusion in widely circulated church manuals, the New Hampshire Confession became the template for thousands of congregational statements of faith, and it is the direct ancestor of the Southern Baptist Convention's Baptist Faith and Message of 1925, 1963, and 2000. If you have ever read the doctrinal statement in the back of a Baptist church's bylaws, you have probably read this document's grandchildren.

What follows is a condensed summary of its articles, a faithful paraphrase, not the full text, though the original is itself brief and worth reading whole. Its opening definition of Scripture, 'truth, without any mixture of error, for its matter,' became one of the most quoted sentences in American church life. The confession's genius is its restraint. It says what Baptists held in common and stops. There is a discipline in that which longer documents, and louder eras, have not always kept.
text:
The following is a condensed summary of the Confession's articles. It is a faithful paraphrase, not the full text.

Article 1. Of the Scriptures. The Holy Bible was written by men divinely inspired, and is a perfect treasure of heavenly instruction; it has God for its author, salvation for its end, and truth, without any mixture of error, for its matter; it reveals the principles by which God will judge us, and is therefore the true center of Christian union and the supreme standard by which all human conduct, creeds, and opinions should be tried.

Article 2. Of the True God. There is one, and only one, living and true God, an infinite, intelligent Spirit, whose name is Jehovah, the Maker and Supreme Ruler of heaven and earth; inexpressibly glorious in holiness, and worthy of all possible honor, confidence, and love; revealed in the unity of the Godhead as three persons — the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost — equal in every divine perfection, and executing distinct but harmonious offices in the great work of redemption.

Article 3. Of the Fall of Man. Man was created in holiness, under the law of his Maker; but by voluntary transgression fell from that holy and happy state; in consequence of which all mankind are now sinners, not by constraint but choice, being by nature utterly void of that holiness required by the law of God, positively inclined to evil, and therefore under just condemnation to eternal ruin, without defense or excuse.

Article 4. Of the Way of Salvation. The salvation of sinners is wholly of grace, through the mediatorial offices of the Son of God, who by the appointment of the Father freely took upon him our nature, yet without sin; honored the divine law by his personal obedience, and by his death made a full atonement for our sins; having risen from the dead, he is now enthroned in heaven, and is in every way qualified to be a suitable, a compassionate, and an all-sufficient Saviour.

Article 5. Of Justification. The great Gospel blessing which Christ secures to such as believe in him is justification; justification includes the pardon of sin and the promise of eternal life on principles of righteousness; it is bestowed not in consideration of any works of righteousness which we have done, but solely through faith in the Redeemer's blood, by virtue of which faith his perfect righteousness is freely imputed to us of God.

Article 6. Of the Freeness of Salvation. The blessings of salvation are made free to all by the Gospel; it is the immediate duty of all to accept them by a cordial, penitent, and obedient faith; and nothing prevents the salvation of the greatest sinner on earth but his own inherent depravity and voluntary rejection of the Gospel, which rejection involves him in an aggravated condemnation.

Article 7. Of Grace in Regeneration. In order to be saved, sinners must be regenerated, or born again; regeneration consists in giving a holy disposition to the mind, and is effected in a manner above our comprehension by the power of the Holy Spirit, in connection with divine truth, so as to secure our voluntary obedience to the Gospel; its proper evidence appears in the holy fruits of repentance, and faith, and newness of life.

Article 8. Of Repentance and Faith. Repentance and faith are sacred duties, and also inseparable graces, wrought in our souls by the regenerating Spirit of God; whereby, being deeply convinced of our guilt, danger, and helplessness, and of the way of salvation by Christ, we turn to God with unfeigned contrition, confession, and supplication for mercy, at the same time heartily receiving the Lord Jesus Christ as our Prophet, Priest, and King, and relying on him alone as the only and all-sufficient Saviour.

Article 9. Of God's Purpose of Grace. Election is the eternal purpose of God, according to which he graciously regenerates, sanctifies, and saves sinners; being perfectly consistent with the free agency of man, it comprehends all the means in connection with the end; it is a most glorious display of God's sovereign goodness, being infinitely free, wise, holy, and unchangeable; it utterly excludes boasting and promotes humility, love, prayer, praise, trust in God, and active imitation of his free mercy; it may be ascertained by its effects in all who truly believe the Gospel.

Article 10. Of Sanctification. Sanctification is the process by which, according to the will of God, we are made partakers of his holiness; it is a progressive work, begun in regeneration, and carried on in the hearts of believers by the presence and power of the Holy Spirit, in the continual use of the appointed means — especially the Word of God, self-examination, self-denial, watchfulness, and prayer.

Article 11. Of the Perseverance of Saints. Such only are real believers as endure unto the end; their persevering attachment to Christ is the grand mark which distinguishes them from superficial professors; a special providence watches over their welfare, and they are kept by the power of God through faith unto salvation.

Article 12. Of the Harmony of the Law and the Gospel. The law of God is the eternal and unchangeable rule of his moral government; it is holy, just, and good; and the inability which the Scriptures ascribe to fallen men to fulfill its precepts arises entirely from their love of sin; to deliver them from which, and to restore them through a Mediator to unfeigned obedience to the holy law, is one great end of the Gospel.

Article 13. Of a Gospel Church. A visible church of Christ is a congregation of baptized believers, associated by covenant in the faith and fellowship of the Gospel; observing the ordinances of Christ; governed by his laws; and exercising the gifts, rights, and privileges invested in them by his Word; its only scriptural officers are bishops, or pastors, and deacons, whose qualifications, claims, and duties are defined in the Epistles to Timothy and Titus.

Article 14. Of Baptism and the Lord's Supper. Christian baptism is the immersion in water of a believer, into the name of the Father, and Son, and Holy Ghost; to show forth, in a solemn and beautiful emblem, our faith in the crucified, buried, and risen Saviour, with its effect in our death to sin and resurrection to a new life; it is prerequisite to the privileges of a church relation, and to the Lord's Supper, in which the members of the church, by the sacred use of bread and wine, are to commemorate together the dying love of Christ, preceded always by solemn self-examination.

Article 15. Of the Christian Sabbath. The first day of the week is the Lord's Day, or Christian Sabbath; it is to be kept sacred to religious purposes, by abstaining from all secular labor and sinful recreations, by the devout observance of all the means of grace, both private and public, and by preparation for that rest that remaineth for the people of God.

Article 16. Of Civil Government. Civil government is of divine appointment, for the interests and good order of human society; magistrates are to be prayed for, conscientiously honored, and obeyed, except only in things opposed to the will of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is the only Lord of the conscience, and the Prince of the kings of the earth.

Article 17. Of the Righteous and the Wicked. There is a radical and essential difference between the righteous and the wicked; such only as through faith are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and sanctified by the Spirit of our God, are truly righteous in his esteem; while all such as continue in impenitence and unbelief are in his sight wicked, and under the curse; and this distinction holds among men both in and after death.

Article 18. Of the World to Come. The end of the world is approaching; at the last day Christ will descend from heaven and raise the dead from the grave to final retribution; a solemn separation will then take place; the wicked will be adjudged to endless punishment, and the righteous to endless joy; and this judgment will fix forever the final state of men, in heaven or hell, on principles of righteousness.

annotations.phrase: truth, without any mixture of error, for its matter
annotations.note: The most influential sentence in the confession. This phrase was carried verbatim into the Baptist Faith and Message and has anchored a century of Baptist debate over biblical inerrancy. A New Hampshire pastor's sentence from 1833 still sets the terms.

annotations.phrase: the true center of Christian union
annotations.note: For a people without bishops, councils, or binding creeds, unity has to rest somewhere. The confession locates it in Scripture itself, which is why Baptist confessions always describe themselves as testimonies of what churches believe, never as rules over them.

The confession's careful diplomacy on display. It affirms total depravity ('utterly void of that holiness') while insisting sinners sin freely. The older Calvinists could sign it. The revivalists could preach it. The wording is the peace treaty.

annotations.phrase: made free to all by the Gospel
annotations.note: Article 6 answers the standing accusation against Calvinists: that election makes evangelism dishonest. The offer is free to all, the duty to believe universal, and the only obstacle is the sinner's own refusal. Brown wrote with Free Will Baptist neighbors looking over his shoulder.

annotations.phrase: perfectly consistent with the free agency of man
annotations.note: Election affirmed, then immediately qualified: sovereign, gracious, unchangeable, yet doing no violence to human freedom, and known only 'by its effects.' You discover your election by believing, not by speculating. This is doctrine written by pastors who had counseled the anxious.

annotations.phrase: a congregation of baptized believers, associated by covenant
annotations.note: The Baptist doctrine of the church in one clause: a local, visible body, composed of the credibly converted, joined by mutual covenant rather than by geography or birth. Every membership roll and church covenant in Baptist life descends from this sentence.

annotations.phrase: the immersion in water of a believer
annotations.note: Both Baptist distinctives in eight words: the mode (immersion) and the subject (a believer). The confession then calls baptism 'prerequisite to the privileges of a church relation,' which is why Baptist churches historically required immersion before membership and the Table.

annotations.phrase: Such only are real believers as endure unto the end
annotations.note: Perseverance stated pastorally rather than speculatively: endurance is the mark that separates real believers from 'superficial professors.' The doctrine comforts the persevering and warns the presuming, in a single sentence.

annotations.phrase: the only Lord of the conscience
annotations.note: The old Baptist fire, banked but burning. Civil government deserves honor and obedience, except where it commands what Christ forbids. People whose great-grandparents were whipped in Massachusetts for their baptisms did not forget to include this.
